forces: Trumpets, horns, oboes, bassoon, strings and continuo
performers: Marine Chamber Orchestra of the United States Marine Band; Major Michelle Rakers, conductor
question: How does a slow dance change colour when the brass drop out?
intro: A slow movement in three beats for the full orchestra, with trumpets and horns holding long notes under the oboes and violins. The first strain is played twice, a second strain without brass follows, and the first strain returns to end the movement.

sections.label: First hearing of the first strain
Da capo · first strain once more
sections.mNote: first strain again, played once, ending on the fermata chord

cues.title: Slowly, in three
cues.text: Lentement is French for “slowly”: a movement in 3/4 for the full orchestra. Trumpets and horns trade long held notes while oboes and violins carry the tune, and figures under the bass line tell the harpsichord which chords to fill in. The first strain is played twice.
cues.evidence: Arnold’s 1788 score, pp. 47–49 (heading Lentement, time signature 3/4, figures under the bass) and HHA pp. 51–52: tied minims in the trumpets in bars 3–4 and in the horns in bars 5–6, a repeat sign after bar 19, and a lowest stave headed Bassi (Violoncello, Violone, Cembalo). The Marine Band’s video of the Bourrée shows a harpsichord at stage left.

cues.title: Fermata, then the strain again
cues.text: The first strain ends on a chord held under a fermata. The sound falls to near silence for about 0.8 seconds, then the strain begins again from its upbeat. The repeat takes 32.8 seconds against 32.5 for the first hearing, so it is a plain repeat at the same pace.
cues.evidence: The relative level falls to −37.7 dB between 33.53 and 34.34 s and to −41.4 dB between 67.13 and 68.10 s. The first hearing runs from about 0.9 to 33.5 s and the repeat from 34.3 to 67.1 s, and their pitch-class content follows each other closely. HHA bar 19 carries the fermata and a repeat sign.

cues.title: The brass fall silent
cues.text: For the second strain trumpets and horns rest for all fifteen bars; oboes, bassoon and strings carry it alone, and the average level falls from about −7 to −12 dB. The audio estimates read B minor at 1:10, E minor near 1:25 and A major at 1:35.
cues.evidence: HHA bars 20–34: the trumpet and horn staves are empty. The mean relative level is −6.6 dB for 39–66 s and −11.6 dB for 69–97 s. Local-key estimates in the audio report: B minor (r 0.89) at 1:10; B major (0.75, 0.77) at 1:15–1:20; E minor (0.78, 0.87) at 1:25–1:30; A major (0.79) at 1:35. These are estimates, not chord identifications.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Da capo, and where it stops
cues.text: After a brief silence the da capo sends the players back to the beginning. The brass return and the first strain is played once more, without its repeat, stopping on the fermata chord marked Fine; the chord is held until about 2:13.
cues.evidence: The relative level falls to −45.1 dB between 97.36 and 98.59 s and is −3.1 dB at 99.0 s; it falls below −22 dB at 133.5 s. HHA bar 34 is marked da capo and bar 19 Fine.

transitions.title: Fermata chord, then the strain again
transitions.how: The first strain ends at bar 19 on a chord held under a fermata in every part, followed by a repeat sign. In the recording the sound falls to about −38 dB for 0.8 seconds, long enough for a breath, before the upbeat of bar 1 starts again. The repeat keeps the full scoring, trumpets and horns included, and the same pace.
transitions.evidence: The relative level falls to −37.7 dB between 33.53 and 34.34 s. HHA bar 19 (fermata and repeat sign); Arnold’s 1788 score, p. 48, where the first strain ends on a fermata chord.

transitions.title: The brass drop out of the second strain
transitions.how: The second hearing of the first strain ends on the same fermata chord (the level is −41 dB at 67.1–68.1 s). The second strain, bars 20–34, starts with trumpets and horns silent and keeps them silent to the end, so oboes, bassoon and strings carry it alone. The audio estimates read B minor at 1:10, E minor around 1:25–1:30 and A major at 1:35: a route from D through the relative minor towards the dominant.
transitions.evidence: HHA bars 19–34 and Arnold’s 1788 score, pp. 48–49, where the trumpet and horn staves are empty in the second strain. The level falls to −41.4 dB at 67.13–68.10 s. The key readings are audio estimates, used as confirmation only.

transitions.title: Da capo returns the opening strain
transitions.how: The second strain ends in silence (about −45 dB at 97.4–98.6 s). Da capo sends the players back to bar 1; the brass return and the level climbs again to the opening’s −3 to −6 dB. The strain is played once, without its repeat, and stops on the D major fermata chord that ended it the first time, marked Fine.
transitions.evidence: The relative level falls to −45.1 dB between 97.36 and 98.59 s. HHA bar 34 (da capo) and bar 19 (Fine); Arnold’s 1788 score, p. 49 (Da Capo).

source.title: Handel, The Celebrated Water-musick in score (London: Samuel Arnold, 1788), pp. 47–49
source.locator: Commons images 25–26 of 30 (BnF). Parts, fermata, repeat sign and da capo checked there; bar numbers follow the Hallische Händel-Ausgabe (Bärenreiter, 1962; IMSLP #559922, printed pp. 51–52), whose structure the recording matches (first strain bars 1–19, repeated; second strain bars 20–34 without brass; da capo to the Fine at bar 19). The performing edition is not identified and the programme lists no players, so entries show the parts printed in the score. The recording is about five decibels louder in the strains that include the brass than in the second strain, which fits their presence; oboes and bassoon are taken from the score.

timeline.note: Full scoring from the first bar: trumpets and horns trade long held notes under the oboes and violins (bars 1–19).
The first strain is repeated with the same scoring.
Trumpets and horns rest for the whole second strain (bars 20–34).
Da capo: the full scoring returns for the first strain, played once more.
The final chord has died away.

fields.note: Commons gives the conductor as Major Michelle Rakers; the programme prints Major Michelle A. Rakers. No roster of individual players is published in the consulted sources. This video’s frames show the conductor and the strings; the ensemble’s harpsichord, bassoon and trumpet are visible in the other movements’ videos, and no frame shows horns or oboes.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Performing edition not identified. The movement number (14 of the three suites) and the structure heard (first strain of 19 bars played twice, second strain of 15 bars without brass, da capo to the fermata chord) match the Hallische Händel-Ausgabe text; no editor or continuo realisation is credited.
fields.note: The programme and Commons name the work and movement numbers but no edition. The structure follows from the measured silences and the Hallische Händel-Ausgabe (Redlich, 1962), which prints 34 bars with a fermata, the mark Fine and a repeat sign at bar 19 and da capo at bar 34; IMSLP’s tally of 34 bars (53 with da capo) agrees.

composer.epithet: A German-trained composer of Italian opera who made the English chorus an actor in public musical drama.
facts: With Friedrich Wilhelm Zachow in Halle; theatre work in Hamburg; study and commissions in Italy, 1706–10
Hanover briefly; settled in London in 1712; became a British subject in 1727
Italian operas, English oratorios, anthems, concertos, chamber cantatas and ceremonial orchestral music
composer.background:
Handel grew up in Halle, the son of a barber-surgeon, and studied with Friedrich Wilhelm Zachow, organist of the town’s principal church. Zachow’s teaching included counterpoint, keyboard playing and the copying of other composers’ music. Handel briefly enrolled at the university and held an organist’s post before moving to Hamburg in 1703. Its public opera house offered a different education: he played in the orchestra and encountered the practical demands of singers, stage machinery and mixed theatrical repertory. His first opera, Almira, was performed there in 1705, with a German text incorporating Italian arias.

From 1706 to 1710 Handel worked in Italy, writing cantatas, sacred music and opera for patrons in Florence, Rome, Naples and Venice. Rome gave him access to virtuoso singers and to instrumentalists associated with Corelli. The Latin Dixit Dominus of 1707 demands rapid, independent choral lines and sustained control of dissonance; the chamber cantatas make emotional turns within much smaller forces. Agrippina, performed in Venice at the end of 1709, assembles much previously written material into a calculated theatrical comedy. Reuse was already part of his method: a successful musical gesture could acquire a different function when assigned to a new character and situation.
